blogs.title: ‘Will Santos Say It?’ and the Reasonable Observer: Transformative Use After Warhol
blogs.description: This post unpacks the Second Circuit’s fair use analysis, emphasizing its reliance on the reasonable observer standard post-Warhol. It explains why Kimmel’s segments were deemed transformative—commenting on Santos’s willingness to say absurd things for money—regardless of Santos’s or Kimmel’s subjective intent. It also examines the court’s treatment of alleged bad faith in obtaining the videos, situating Harper & Row’s “good faith” language within contemporary doctrine and showing why deception did not defeat fair use here.

blogs.title: Fair Use at the Pleading Stage: The Second Circuit’s Growing Comfort with Early Dismissals
blogs.description: Focusing on procedure, this post analyzes the court’s willingness to resolve fair use on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, drawing on TCA Television, Cariou, and Hachette. It discusses how the panel relied on the complaint, incorporated exhibits, and judicial notice of copyright registrations to find fair use as a matter of law. The post assesses the implications for media defendants and plaintiffs, including how detailed pleading and evidentiary attachments can influence early outcomes.

blogs.title: Markets, Mockery, and Cameo: Why the Fourth Factor Cut Against Santos
blogs.description: This piece examines the market-harm analysis, highlighting the court’s distinction between market substitution and devaluation through criticism. It explains why a late-night mocking segment does not usurp the licensing market for Cameo videos and how Campbell’s skepticism toward licensing markets for criticism applies. The post also considers the ‘nature’ and ‘amount’ factors in context, including the videos’ publication status and the necessity of using enough of the work to make the commentary intelligible.

blogs.title: Platform Terms Won’t Save You: The Collapse of Santos’s State-Law Claims
blogs.description: This post explores the failure of Santos’s contract and fraud theories. It explains why Santos could not enforce Cameo’s Terms of Service as a third-party beneficiary under Illinois law, why his implied-in-fact contract claim faltered under New York law for lack of concrete terms and a meeting of the minds, and why his fraudulent inducement claim failed for want of out-of-pocket loss. It closes with practical takeaways for creators and public figures who rely on platform terms to police downstream use.
